entries.title: Place value and changing bases
entries.text: A numeral is just a row of symbols. What turns it into a number is place value: every position has a weight, and the value is the sum of digit × weight over all positions. Digits and places Think of an odometer. The right-hand wheel counts single units; each time it rolls past its last symbol it nudges the wheel to its left by one. In base ten that happens after 9, in base two after 1. The wheel a digit sits on decides how much it is worth. In base b (an integer b \ge 2) a numeral d_k d_{k-1} \dots d_1 d_0 uses digits 0 \le d_i < b, and the digit in position i (counting from 0 at the right) is worth d_i \cdot b^{\,i}. The word radix means the same thing as base. Exam papers use both. Expanding a numeral Add up the weighted digits: N = \sum_{i=0}^{k} d_i\, b^{\,i} = d_k b^k + d_{k-1} b^{k-1} + \dots + d_1 b + d_0 . Pull out a factor of b from every term except the last, then repeat inside the brackets: N = \Big( \big( (d_k\, b + d_{k-1})\, b + d_{k-2} \big) b + \dots \Big) b + d_0 . The second form needs only one multiplication and one addition per digit. Every whole number N \ge 0 has exactly one numeral in base b without leading zeros. All terms of the expansion except d_0 are multiples of b, so d_0 must be the remainder of N divided by b, and that remainder is a single, fixed digit. Removing it leaves (N - d_0)/b, a smaller whole number, which by the same argument has a fixed last digit too. Repeating until nothing is left pins down every digit, so two different numerals cannot have the same value. (257)_8 = 2 \cdot 64 + 5 \cdot 8 + 7 = 128 + 40 + 7 = 175. If (31)_b = 16, then 3b + 1 = 16, so b = 5. Check that every digit is below the base: 3 < 5 and 1 < 5. ✓ What is (110)_2 in decimal? 1 \cdot 4 + 1 \cdot 2 + 0 = 6. To read a binary string in your head, start at 0 and, for each bit from left to right, double the running total and add the bit. For 1011: 0 \to 1 \to 2 \to 5 \to 11. This is the bracketed form from the derivation, done one step at a time. A digit must be smaller than the base. "(19)_8" is not an octal numeral at all, and an equation such as (43)_x = (y3)_8 silently requires x > 4 and y < 8. Practice The same idea extends to the right of the point: the first fractional position is worth b^{-1}, the next b^{-2}, and so on. You will need this for fixed-point questions. A digit's value is digit × b^{\text{position}}; positions count from 0 at the right. Every digit must be less than the base. Read numerals fast with the nested form \big((d_k b + d_{k-1}) b + \dots\big) b + d_0.
